narr: In this section, we'll explore the concept of models in engineering, focusing on how they help us understand complex systems.
We'll look at different types of models, their components, and how to apply them to real-world problems like electric campus buses.

data.heading: Models in Engineering
bullets: Models are simplified representations of systems that help answer specific questions
Two maps mentioned: Power diagram (switching/isolation) and Geographic diagram (distances/locations)
Neither map is the network itself, but each serves a purpose
Epigraph: 'All models are wrong, but some are useful.' - George Box

narr: What exactly do we mean by models in engineering? Well, think of them as simplified pictures of complex systems that help us answer specific questions.
For example, consider two different maps of a power network. The power diagram tells us about switching and isolation, while the geographic diagram shows distances and locations.
Importantly, neither map is the actual network itself, but each serves a purpose for different types of questions.
As statistician George Box famously said, 'All models are wrong, but some are useful.' This captures the essence of modeling - we simplify to gain understanding.

data.heading: Four Types of Models
bullets: Physical - scaled-down or simplified objects (e.g., wind turbine blade in a wind tunnel)
Graphical - diagrams showing parts and connections (e.g., one-line diagram)
Mathematical - equations relating variables (e.g., Ohm's law)
Computational - step-by-step calculations (e.g., electricity demand table)

narr: Engineering projects typically use four types of models. First, physical models are real, scaled-down copies of systems, like a wind turbine blade tested in a wind tunnel.
Second, graphical models are diagrams that show parts and connections, such as one-line electrical diagrams or energy-flow diagrams.
Third, mathematical models use equations to relate variables, like Ohm's law for electrical circuits.
Finally, computational models involve step-by-step calculations performed by computers, such as tables of hourly electricity demand.
Real projects often mix several types - using diagrams to organize, equations to compute, and tables to run the numbers.

data.heading: One System - Three Models
bullets: Campus electricity supply can be modeled in three different ways
One-line diagram (graphical): answers 'which buildings lose power when a feeder is switched off?'
Energy balance equation (mathematical): answers 'does daily generation cover daily demand?'
Hourly demand table (computational): answers 'in which hour does the peak occur?'

narr: Consider the campus electricity supply system. We can model this same system in three different ways, depending on what question we want to answer.
First, a one-line diagram (graphical model) tells us which buildings lose power when a feeder is switched off, but it omits distances and power ratings.
Second, an energy balance equation (mathematical model) tells us if daily generation covers daily demand, but it doesn't tell us when that demand occurs.
Third, an hourly demand table (computational model) tells us when peak demand occurs, but it doesn't show the network diagram or voltages.
The key point is: one system, three models - the question decides which one to use.

data.heading: Anatomy of a Model: Four Parts
bullets: Inputs - values we choose or can change (battery size, speed, route length)
Parameters - numbers kept fixed (energy consumption per km, usable battery share)
Relationships - rules linking numbers (Energy = energy per km × distance)
Outputs - what the model predicts (range in km, energy in kWh/day)

narr: Every model, regardless of type, consists of four essential parts. First, inputs are the values we choose or can change, like battery size or route length.
Second, parameters are numbers kept fixed, like energy consumption per kilometer or the usable share of the battery.
Third, relationships are the rules that link these numbers, such as the equation Energy equals energy per kilometer times distance.
Fourth, outputs are what the model predicts - the results we evaluate, like range in kilometers or energy in kilowatt-hours per day.
Think of a model as a machine: numbers go in, a rule is applied, and numbers come out. And every number needs its own units.

data.heading: Model Variables and Their Roles
bullets: Performance variables → outputs (range per charge [km], energy per day [kWh/day])
Design variables → inputs (battery capacity [kWh], number of buses)
Context variables → parameters (route length [km], air temperature [°C], charging hours)

narr: Interestingly, the variables we identified in week 4 become the roles in our model this week. Performance variables, like range per charge or energy per day, become outputs of our model.
Design variables, like battery capacity or number of buses, become inputs we can control.
And context variables, like route length or air temperature, become parameters we keep fixed.

data.heading: Need-Know-How-Solve Method
bullets: Need - the variable we want (range per charge, km)
Know - what is already known (battery capacity, usable share, consumption per km)
How - the model and assumptions (Range = usable energy ÷ energy per km)
Solve - compute, check units, interpret results

narr: The method we'll use this week is called Need-Know-How-Solve. First, identify what you need to find - the variable you want, like range per charge in kilometers.
Second, determine what you already know - the battery capacity, usable share, and consumption per kilometer.
Third, develop the model and state your assumptions - in this case, that range equals usable energy divided by energy per kilometer.
Finally, solve by computing, checking units, and interpreting the results. Importantly, the 'How' step includes the assumptions you make, which might be hidden.
Let's look at the specific equations for our electric bus model. The trip energy E equals the consumption e times the distance d.
The range R equals the usable energy u times the battery capacity C, divided by the consumption e.

Where C is the battery capacity in kilowatt-hours, u is the usable share (a unitless number between 0 and 1), e is the consumption in kilowatt-hours per kilometer, and d is the distance in kilometers.
The range R will be in kilometers, and the trip energy E in kilowatt-hours.
A unit check confirms this: u times C gives kilowatt-hours, divided by e in kilowatt-hours per kilometer, gives kilometers for the range.
For example, with a 160 kilowatt-hour usable energy divided by 1.2 kilowatt-hours per kilometer, we get a range of 133 kilometers.

data.heading: Problem 1 — Electric Bus Range Calculation
data.problem: Calculate the range of an electric campus bus with the following specifications: battery capacity C = 200 kWh, usable share u = 0.8, consumption e = 1.2 kWh/km. The daily route is 8 laps of 12 km each.

steps.text: Calculate usable energy: u × C = 0.8 × 200 kWh = 160 kWh
Calculate range: R = (u × C) ÷ e = 160 kWh ÷ 1.2 kWh/km = 133.33 km
Calculate daily energy requirement: 8 laps × 12 km/lap × 1.2 kWh/km = 115.2 kWh
Calculate daily distance: 8 laps × 12 km/lap = 96 km
Compare range to daily distance: 133.33 km > 96 km

data.result: The bus has a range of 133.33 km on a full charge, which covers the daily requirement of 96 km with a margin of approximately 37.33 km.

narr: Let's apply our model to a specific problem. We need to calculate the range of an electric campus bus with a 200 kilowatt-hour battery, 80% usable share, and consumption of 1.2 kilowatt-hours per kilometer.
First, we calculate the usable energy by multiplying the battery capacity by the usable share: 0.8 times 200 kilowatt-hours equals 160 kilowatt-hours.
Next, we calculate the range by dividing the usable energy by the consumption: 160 kilowatt-hours divided by 1.2 kilowatt-hours per kilometer equals approximately 133.33 kilometers.
We then calculate the daily energy requirement: 8 laps of 12 kilometers each, multiplied by the consumption rate, gives us 115.2 kilowatt-hours per day.
The daily distance is simply 8 laps times 12 kilometers per lap, which equals 96 kilometers.
Comparing the range to the daily distance, we see that 133.33 kilometers is greater than 96 kilometers, meaning one charge covers the day with a margin of about 37.33 kilometers.

data.heading: Three Kinds of Assumptions
bullets: Simplifying - what we ignore (hills, traffic lights, stops, driver differences)
Data - what we fix (e = 1.2 kWh/km; C = 200 kWh; u = 0.8)
Boundary - what we leave outside (passengers, charger, grid; only the bus is in the model)

narr: But how far can we trust this number? That depends on the assumptions we made. There are three kinds of assumptions to consider.
First, simplifying assumptions are what we choose to ignore - like hills, traffic lights, stops, or differences between drivers.
Second, data assumptions are what we fix - like using e = 1.2 kWh/km, C = 200 kWh, and u = 0.8.
Third, boundary assumptions determine what we leave outside our model - in this case, we're only considering the bus itself, not passengers, the charger, or the grid.
Remember from week 2: the boundary is a choice, and every assumption is a choice too.

data.heading: Template for Writing Assumptions
bullets: Format: 'We assume [assumption] because [reason]. If it is wrong, [effect on result]'
Example: 'We assume 1.2 kWh/km in all seasons, because we only have autumn test data. If wrong, winter range may fall below the daily requirement of 96 km'
Assumptions should be written down so they can be checked
Hidden assumptions cannot be verified

narr: The course provides a specific template for writing assumptions: 'We assume [assumption] because [reason]. If it is wrong, [effect on result]'

For example: 'We assume 1.2 kilowatt-hours per kilometer in all seasons, because we only have autumn test data. If this assumption is wrong, the winter range may fall below the daily requirement of 96 kilometers.'
When writing assumptions, ask yourself: will a teammate be able to understand what you ignored, fixed, and left outside? Can it be checked?
The key point is that an assumption that is written down can be checked, but a hidden one cannot.

data.heading: Key Takeaways
items: Models are simplified representations that help answer specific questions
Four types: physical, graphical, mathematical, computational
Every model has four parts: inputs, parameters, relationships, outputs
Use Need-Know-How-Solve method for systematic modeling
Document all assumptions using the provided template

narr: Let's summarize what we've learned about models in engineering. First, models are simplified representations that help us answer specific questions about complex systems.
Second, there are four types of models: physical, graphical, mathematical, and computational, each serving different purposes.
Third, every model has four essential parts: inputs, parameters, relationships, and outputs.
Fourth, the Need-Know-How-Solve method provides a systematic approach to modeling problems.
Finally, it's crucial to document all assumptions using the provided template, making them explicit and checkable.
